content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about your project to understand the needs clearly and support development effectively. Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations differ?

Yes, that sounds in line with what we need. We’re looking to clarify the needs for the standalone triangulation games application, including how people will play, how new game types get added, and what the interface should support.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking on behalf of the research team that wants this application for studying and playing triangulation-based combinatorial games. I’m involved because we need to make sure the tool supports both players and game developers, and that it can be extended without rebuilding the whole system each time.
Thank you. How would you describe this project in two to four sentences?

This project is a standalone application for playing combinatorial games based on triangulations. It should let different kinds of users play alone, against a computer opponent, or with another person through a graphical interface that’s easy to use. It also needs to support adding new games so developers can extend the system without changing the original application.
Could you describe the current process or system you use for playing, testing, or extending these triangulation-based games?

Right now it’s pretty fragmented. People usually rely on separate research tools, handwritten rules, or custom scripts to test ideas, and extending a game tends to mean making code changes in whatever prototype we’re using. There isn’t a single shared application that handles play, experimentation, and adding new game variants in one place.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what are the main features you hope to get from this project?

We want to replace the ad hoc setup with one consistent application that makes it easy to start a game, choose a game type, and play without needing technical setup. We also want computer opponents and two-player play to work smoothly, plus a clear way for developers to define new games and publish them into the app. The big improvement is reducing the amount of custom coding and manual coordination needed for each new game or experiment.

So the main features are: a consistent standalone app, easy game start and game-type selection, solo play, computer opponents, two-player play, and a developer-friendly way to define and publish new games without modifying the core application — is that right?
Yes, that’s right. That captures the main features and the overall direction we want for the project.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project that we haven’t mentioned yet?

A few things would be nice if they fit naturally, like saving and restoring games, and maybe some way to inspect or review moves after a game ends. I’d also expect basic help or guidance in the interface so people who aren’t technical can still get started easily.
Based on your description, do you think support for saving and restoring games should also be included?
Yes, I think it should be included. It would make the app much more practical for longer games and for research sessions where people need to pause and come back later.

Could you please prioritize these main features for me: the standalone app, easy game-type selection and starting a game, solo play, computer opponents, two-player play, developer-defined new games, saving/restoring games, move review after a game, and basic help/guidance?

The top priority is the standalone app itself, along with easy game-type selection and starting a game, because that’s the core experience we need right away. Next I’d put solo play, computer opponents, and two-player play, since those are the main ways people will actually use it, followed by developer-defined new games so the system can grow. Saving and restoring games, basic help, and move review are important too, but I’d treat those as secondary enhancements unless they’re needed to make the core use cases workable.
Please visualize the first page of your application and explain how you would interact with it step-by-step.

The first page should be a very simple start screen with the game title at the top, a clear list or dropdown for choosing the game type, and obvious buttons for starting a new game or continuing a saved one. I’d also want a small help link or panel on the same page so someone new can understand what to do without hunting around. After choosing the game type, I’d pick the play mode, such as solo, against the computer, or two players, then press start and go straight into the board.
Could you describe the current process you’d want for adding a new game type into the application?

Ideally, a developer would define the new game in some external way, like a configuration or plugin package, and then register it so the application can discover it at startup. They should not have to change the core code just to add a new game type, and it should appear in the game selection list once it’s installed. If there’s any validation or metadata needed, I’d expect the app to check that when the new game is loaded.
Please elaborate on what you want this new-game definition to accomplish, especially what information it needs to contain for the application to load and offer the game correctly.

It needs enough information for the app to know the game’s identity, how to present it to the user, and how the rules engine should initialize it. I’d expect at least a name, a short description, the supported play modes, and whatever setup parameters the game needs to build the initial triangulation and validate moves. If the game has any special restrictions or extra metadata, that should be included too so the app can show it correctly and reject invalid setups.

It seems like you need a game definition containing the game’s name, description, supported play modes, initialization/setup parameters, move-validation rules, and any special restrictions or metadata. Can you describe more about how a player should save and restore a game, or what should be included in a saved game file?

A saved game should capture exactly enough to continue from the same point without ambiguity. I’d expect it to store the selected game type, the full board state, whose turn it is, the move history if that matters for review, and any settings or parameters that affect the rules. If there’s anything game-specific that could change how the position is interpreted, that should be included too so restoring is reliable.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

The main people beyond the players are the game developers who will define and extend new games, because the application has to fit their workflow without forcing core code changes. Researchers are also important since this is for combinatorial games and they may care about reproducibility, saving states, and reviewing moves afterward. I’d also include the less technical users, because the interface and guidance need to be simple enough that they can start a game and play without learning the underlying system first.
What would you consider a successful deployment of this application, in practical terms for your team?

A successful deployment would mean the app installs and runs reliably on the target systems, and users can immediately pick a game, start playing, and save or restore without issues. It would also mean developers can add a new game and see it show up correctly without needing a patched build. For our team, success is really that the core gameplay and extension workflow work smoothly enough that people can use it in practice without hand-holding.

To summarize, we discussed a standalone triangulation games application with easy game selection and startup, solo play, computer opponents, two-player play, external/new-game definitions without core-code changes, saving and restoring games, move review, and basic help/guidance. Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is that the interface should stay accessible and not assume users are technically confident. I’d also like the app to handle errors gracefully, especially if a game definition is invalid or a saved game can’t be loaded, and explain what went wrong in plain language. Beyond that, I think the main needs we’ve discussed cover the important parts.
